title: A Somber Yet Hopeful Holiday Blessing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing at the close of a hard semester, Stuart reaches for Dorothy Sayers's distinction between the pragmatist who treats life as a problem to solve and the artist who treats it as a medium for creation, and argues teachers need more of the latter stance heading into the new year. He uses Picasso's Guernica — painted in response to a bombing he was powerless to stop — as a parable for teachers who feel outmatched by the forces working against their students' hearts. The devastated Spanish town becomes a metaphor for what dehumanizing school systems and hard circumstances can do to a child's inner life by the time they reach a teacher's classroom. Stuart doesn't pretend art (or teaching) fixes the underlying tragedy, but insists the act of creating in spite of that tragedy still matters immensely. The piece closes as a blessing: a wish that teachers carry an artist's faith in the value of their work into the new year, regardless of whether outcomes are visible or immediate.
points: Stuart frames the teacher's stance choice as Sayers' pragmatist ("life as a problem to be solved") versus her artist ("life as a medium for creation") — arguing the second stance sustains teachers better through circumstances they can't fix.

Picasso's Guernica functions as proof that creative response to devastation has lasting value even when it doesn't prevent further devastation, a reframe for teachers who feel their work is too small to matter against systemic harm.
The essay explicitly names school systems' capacity for dehumanization as a source of the "bombed out" hearts teachers inherit in their students, without pretending a single classroom can undo it.
The piece models the "colleague" register Stuart uses across the blog — direct pastoral address rather than instructional content — positioning holiday reflections as their own genre of the archive.
quotes: It's not bad to seek to solve problems — not at all. But there is just that persnickety quality of human life that's so hard for modern folks to accept: we're finite. We have only so much time, so much energy, so much influence.

But colleague — those two pictures are what's happened in the hearts of so many of our hurting students. They all started out life as this pristine and beautiful little cosmos — this precious village between the hills.

But by the time they've come to us, there's more than a fair share of them whose hearts look like that second picture — bombed out by external factors, one of which is most definitely a school system that can tend toward dehumanization.
What's an artist to do, when faced with such darkness and power? What value does a paintbrush have against bombs and cruelty?" And what he did is, he decided to paint.
And so, my year-end prayer and wish for you and me is this: that our approach to our work come January would be more like Sayers' artist and less like the pragmatist.
But when we zoom out all the way, I hope we'll see the artistry of what we do, sometimes within and in congruence with our circumstances, and sometimes underneath and despite them.
